title: Adopting Fast and Slow: Cross-Country Evidence on Business Adoption of Artificial Intelligence
text:
## Adopting Fast and Slow: Cross-Country Evidence on Business Adoption of Artificial Intelligence

Elwyn Davies, David Francis, Filip Jolevski, Gaurav Nayyar, Katherine Stapleton and Shu Yu World Bank1

Background paper prepared for World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence www.worldbank.org/en/publication/wdr2026

Abstract This paper presents ten stylized facts on the use of Artificial Intelligence drawn from nationally representative surveys of 4,205 firms in seven economies: India, Jordan, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria, Thailand, and the United States. The findings indicate a fast trend in the adoption of AI by firms across the world. Evidence suggests that AI is used for a wide range of business tasks and functions, consistent with it being a General-Purpose Technology. While AI adoption rates of firms nearly tripled between 2024 and 2025, suggesting a fast diffusion, the diffusion of sophisticated use cases remains more slowly and highly concentrated. The early evidence shows little impact on labor markets in developing economies, while in contrast layoffs and hiring freezes due to AI are more common in the U.S. Looking forward, firm managers expect AI adoption to positively affect their employment levels and productivity over the next three years.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence; AI adoption; firms; technology sophistication. 
JEL codes: O33, O57; O14; D22.

## 1 Introduction

Cross-country adoption data suggests that Generative AI (GenAI) has been diffusing around the world 
faster than other technologies since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022 (Chatterji et al. 2025; Appel et al. 2025). 
Nevertheless there remains a significant knowledge gap on the extent of firm-level adoption of AI, how the 
technology is being used by different types of firms, and its impacts on the firms adopting it. While some 
studies have directly estimated the share of firms using AI through surveys, efforts so far have focused on 
the U.S. and a handful of high-income countries (McElheran et al. 2025, Bonney et al. 2026, Yotzov et al. 
2026, Eurostat 2026), and results largely depend on the scope of AI under consideration, who the 
respondents are (e.g., senior executives vs. frontline workers), the sample coverage, and the weighting 
scheme (Li et al. 2026). This knowledge gap is particularly acute for developing countries, where to date 
there is very little empirical evidence on how AI is being adopted or its impacts. 
This paper aims to address this knowledge gap by shedding new light on how firms around the world are 
adopting AI. It presents ten findings with new and early evidence on AI adoption from nationally 
representative surveys of 4205 firms in seven countries: the U.S., Thailand, Mexico, Nigeria, India, Jordan, 
and Kenya. It shows that the use of AI has grown rapidly in firms around the world, with developing 
countries seeing nearly the same growth rate in adoption as in the U.S. In the six developing economies 
surveyed, usage of AI has increased from 1 percent in 2020 to 27 percent by 2025, just behind the U.S.’s 
level of 40 percent in 2025. The diffusion of AI among firms has been faster than seen for other key 
technologies, with the adoption curve far steeper for AI than was seen previously for email or websites. 
The most common technologies used are AI chatbots and other generative forms of AI (AI used to generate 
images, sounds, video, or larger pieces of text). Other forms of AI technologies, such as AI agents, AI for 
workflow automation or decision support, and AI for autonomous physical machine movement, remain 
less used. The rapid pace of diffusion could reflect the already high adoption rates of the internet and other 
enabling digital technologies, as firms with higher adoption of other digital technologies are more likely to 
adopt AI. 
AI is used for a wide range of such business tasks, ranging from finding information to controlling business 
or production processes. Among those firms that do use AI, the task with the highest share of firms using 
AI is finding information. By contrast, the task with the lowest share of firms using AI is coding or software. 
The propensity to use AI is notably higher in the surveyed developing countries than in the U.S. when it 
comes to using AI forfinding information, translation, and customer or external interactions. The difference 
suggests that AI plays an important role in further closing language, information, or communication 
barriers facing firms in developing countries. In terms of business functions, the the highest proportion of 
AI-using firms use the technology for marketing, sales, and product development (64 percent of AI-using 
firms in the U.S. and just under 60 percent of AI-using firms in surveyed developing countries), followed 
by research and development. The second-most frequently cited business function among AI users is 
research and development. The results are also consistent with AI being a general-purpose technology 
(GPT): in both the U.S. and surveyed developing countries, there are sizeable and nearly equivalent 
proportions of firms using AI for several (four or more) business functions. 
Although AI has diffused fast, more sophisticated use cases of AI have spread more slowly, and remain 
limited and highly concentrated. This study constructs an index of AI sophistication, consisting of the 
following components: (1) whether a firm adopts any AI technology; (2) whether a firm adopts AI agents, 
AI process automation, or AI-driven robotics; (3) whether a firm uses them for more advanced tasks (such 
as coding); (4) the number of business functions AI is used for; and (5) whether a solution is customized 
(either internally or externally). The results show that firms in the surveyed developing countries deploy 
AI technology in a less sophisticated way than firms in the U.S. The composite AI sophistication index in 
the U.S. is about 70 percent higher than in the surveyed developing countries, with a similar gap found 
across all components of the index. Sophisticated AI adoption is also highly concentrated in large firms. 
In terms of the characteristics of firms adopting AI, AI adoption and AI sophistication are higher for firms 
with higher innovation activity and higher prior digital use. For example, firms with a history of innovation 
through the introduction of new products or services are 17 percentage points more likely to use AI, while 
those investing in R&D are 13 percentage points more likely to do the same. Firms where more than half 
of workers use computers are 35 percentage points more likely to have adopted AI. These findings reinforce 
earlier evidence that firms that were more technologically sophisticated before AI use took off have 
adopted GenAI at much higher rates than less technologically sophisticated firms. The surveys also ask 
which reason, among seven, is their main constraint for not using AI or not increasing use. Across both 
groups—AI adopters and AI non-adopters—a lack of knowledge is the most highly cited constraint. 
The surveys also provide early evidence on the labor market implications of AI by asking firms if they have 
laid off workers due to AI, frozen hiring, reassigned workers or started hiring new workers. In the U.S., 16 
percent of firms report layoffs due to AI adoption, and in the surveyed developing countries, this is lower 
at 7 percent. Nevertheless, roughly a quarter of US firms and 13 percent of firms in the surveyed developing 
countries report slowing or freezing hiring due to AI adoption. Conversely, firms that have adopted AI are 
also more likely to hire and reassign their workers. The share of firms hiring new workers due to AI is 
higher in developing countries than in the US, with 21 percent of firms in the surveyed developing 
countries hiring workers due to AI adoption, which is four times the level observed in the U.S. Despite 
uncertainty about the future, firms generally expect AI adoption to positively affect their employment 
levels and productivity over the next three years. 
This paper contributes to the existing literature on firm-level AI adoption in several ways. First, it adds 
new evidence to the literature measuring the extent and types of firm-level AI adoption in the US or 
advanced economies. For instance, in the U.S., McElheran et al. (2025) show that adoption among U.S. 
manufacturing firms ranged from 13 to 23 percent in 2021, depending on the definition of AI used. More 
recently, the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey reports that 18 percent of U.S. firms 
used AI during November 2025–January 2026 (Bonney et al. 2026. A survey of senior executives using a 
broad definition of AI reports a U.S. firm adoption rate of 78 percent (Yotzov et al. 2026), while Hartley et 
al. (2026) found that 38 percent of U.S. workers reported having adopted an LLM as of December 2025. This 
paper’s finding that 40 percent of U.S. firms (with five or more employees) had adopted AI falls somewhere 
in the middle of these other estimates. 
This paper also contributes to the literature on cross-country AI diffusion. Some international surveys have 
been conducted to enable cross-country comparisons of firm-level AI adoption. For instance, OECD (2025) 
found that between 2020 and 2024, the share of businesses with 10 or more employees using AI increased 
from 6 percent to 14 percent across member countries. Eurostat (2026) carried out harmonized enterprise 
surveys and showed that 20 percent of EU enterprises used at least one AI technology in 2025, with 
adoption rates ranging from 5 percent to 42 percent across member states. Yotzov et al. (2026) conducted 
executive surveys with comparable questions across four countries and reported much higher adoption 
rates than Eurostat (2026), with the highest at 78 percent in the U.S. and the lowest at 59 percent in Australia. 
Our study contributes to this line of research by broadening the cross-country comparison beyond high 
income countries to include developing economies as well. 
Finally, this paper contributes to the literature on the labor market effects of AI. Hui, Reshef and Zhou 
(2024), Teutloff et al. (2025) and Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) all document displacement effects 
of AI for certain groups of workers. Conversely, Humlum and Vestergaard (2025), using Danish 
administrative data, find null effects on earnings and hours, while Hartley et al. (2024) find no statistically 
significant declines in job openings or employment in exposed occupations. Firm-level European evidence 
also points to productivity gains without short-run labor replacement (Aldasoro et al. 2026), and Hampole 
et al. (2025) find positive employment effects of firm-wide adoption masking substantial occupational 
heterogeneity. By directly asking firms whether they have laid off workers due to AI, this paper provides 
evidence on job impacts without relying on a causal identification strategy. Our finding that a small subset
